bounded-limits: You never have all the facts. You never have enough time. And you can only hold a few things in mind at once. So you do not find the best answer — you find one that is good enough, and you move on. That is not a flaw in you. It is what thinking with a real brain costs, and it is true of everyone who has ever been good at anything.

pink-triad: Three things keep a person going at something hard: a reason that matters to them, the feeling of getting better, and some say in how they do it. Take any one away and the same work starts to feel like a slog. That is the idea Daniel Pink set out in his book Drive, and it is worth knowing here because working with AI can move all three at once — and not always in the same direction.

trust-forecast: Trust sounds like a feeling. It works better as a prediction: given what you have seen so far, you expect a person or a tool to behave a certain way — and you change the prediction when new evidence turns up. Faith asks you to commit without evidence. Trust asks you to commit on evidence that is never complete, and to keep paying attention afterwards. So the aim is not to reach the point where you can stop checking. It is to check the things worth checking.

trust-equation-intro: There is a well-known way of picturing it, from The Trusted Advisor by David Maister, Charles Green and Robert Galford. Trust goes up with three things — whether you have shown you know your subject, whether you do what you said you would, and whether people feel safe bringing you something awkward. It goes down with one: how much you seem to be in it for yourself.

trust-fallible: Now the honest part, because it matters more than the formula. That is a way of thinking, not a measurement. None of the four parts arrives with a number, so nothing can really be added or divided. The parts are not even fixed — swap "people feel safe with you" for "people can predict how you decide" and it still works, which tells you they were a choice. And it can point the wrong way: sharing more of yourself is supposed to build trust, and sometimes it does the opposite. Keep it as a picture that helps you notice which part is missing. Do not keep it as a score.

memory-layers: Hold a phone number in your head while you dial it. That is working memory: a handful of things at once, gone in a blink. It is that small for everyone, and practice does not make it bigger. So the useful move is not to hold more — it is to put things somewhere you can reliably find them again. A note. A list. A page that keeps them for you.

memory-linking: Saving things feels like progress, and mostly isn't. A folder of clippings does nothing, because having something filed is not the same as being able to reach it. What changes that is linking: when one note names another, both become easier to find, and the collection gets more useful faster than it gets bigger.

You already have settings for it: what you read, who you listen to, which ideas you wave off before you have really looked. Almost nobody chose those settings on purpose — and they are the part of all this you can most easily change.

three-doors: There are three ways to meet something new, not two. You can shut the door: reject it unless it is already approved. You can take everything in without checking, which is not open-mindedness, just gullibility. Or you can hold off on the no — let it in to be tested, and see whether it survives. Only that third one can correct itself, because the other two never find out they were wrong.
